reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ESC & ACC-AHA guidelines
clinicalPearls: Rheumatic heart disease is the chronic valvular sequel of acute rheumatic fever, an immune-mediated complication of group A streptococcal infection, and remains a major cause of valve disease in many parts of the world
The mitral valve is most often affected, and mitral stenosis is the most characteristic lesion, though mixed mitral and aortic valve involvement is common
Patients may be asymptomatic for years before developing exertional breathlessness, fatigue, palpitations from atrial fibrillation, or features of heart failure
Although the valve damage itself is non-infective, these valves are prone to infective endocarditis, which must be considered when there is fever or clinical deterioration
Mitral stenosis predisposes to atrial fibrillation and left atrial thrombus, and to systemic embolism including stroke
Echocardiography is central to assessing valve morphology, severity, and haemodynamic consequences
Prevention relies on prompt treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis and long-term secondary antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent recurrent rheumatic fever
Advanced disease may require balloon valvuloplasty for suitable mitral stenosis, or surgical repair or valve replacement
reference.pathophysiology: Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis in susceptible individuals, in whom molecular mimicry between streptococcal antigens and host tissue drives a cross-reactive immune response affecting the heart, joints, skin, and nervous system. Recurrent or severe carditis produces chronic inflammation and scarring of the valves, with leaflet thickening, commissural fusion, and chordal shortening. Over years this yields stenosis, regurgitation, or mixed dysfunction, most commonly of the mitral valve. The resulting pressure and volume loading leads to atrial enlargement, atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension, and eventually heart failure.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital valve abnormalities such as bicuspid aortic valve
Non-rheumatic mitral regurgitation from prolapse or ischaemia
Other causes of mitral stenosis such as severe annular calcification
Cardiomyopathy presenting with functional valve regurgitation
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic and, when needed, transoesophageal echocardiography to define valve morphology and severity
12-lead ECG to detect atrial fibrillation and chamber enlargement
Chest radiography for chamber size, pulmonary congestion, and valve calcification
Evidence of prior streptococcal infection and inflammatory markers in suspected acute disease
Assessment of pulmonary pressures and right heart consequences
Blood cultures and endocarditis workup when infection is suspected
redFlags: Fever or systemic features suggesting superimposed infective endocarditis on a damaged valve
New atrial fibrillation with embolic risk, or acute systemic embolism such as stroke
Acute pulmonary oedema or rapidly progressive heart failure
Haemoptysis or severe pulmonary hypertension in advanced mitral stenosis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the valves involved, severity, and access to secondary prophylaxis and intervention; secondary prophylaxis and timely valve intervention allow many patients to do well, but advanced disease with pulmonary hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and heart failure carries significant morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Overlooking superimposed infective endocarditis when a patient with known rheumatic valve disease develops fever
Failing to maintain long-term secondary antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent recurrent rheumatic fever
Underestimating stroke risk from atrial fibrillation and left atrial thrombus in mitral stenosis
Delaying valve intervention until irreversible pulmonary hypertension or ventricular dysfunction has developed
management: Maintain long-term secondary prophylaxis with regular benzathine penicillin to prevent recurrent rheumatic fever
Manage heart-failure symptoms with diuretics and control the rate and rhythm in atrial fibrillation
Anticoagulate with a vitamin K antagonist for atrial fibrillation, left atrial thrombus or a prosthetic valve
Refer for valve intervention (balloon valvuloplasty, repair or replacement) guided by echocardiographic severity and symptoms
Maintain vigilance for infective endocarditis and treat it promptly when suspected
Monitor with serial echocardiography for progression of valve dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension
Coordinate combined cardiology and obstetric care in pregnancy and maintain dental and general health
